content: The institutional capacity for research should be assessed, including the availability of research institutions and resources. The national system for coordinating and overseeing research must be described, highlighting the role of academia, civil society, and community organizations in generating field evidence and translating research into national policy and practice. Specific provisions for research on priority infectious diseases, particularly tuberculosis (TB), should be included. The epidemiology of TB in the country should be detailed using the latest available data. This includes identifying geographical areas with the highest TB burden, comparing TB occurrence in rural versus urban settings, and determining regions or districts with the highest case numbers and notification rates. Relevant data should be presented using appropriate graphics to facilitate the identification of populations and groups requiring focused interventions. The national and subnational burden of TB, including drug-resistant TB, should be outlined. This section should include key impact indicators from the End TB Strategy, such as estimated incidence, mortality, and the proportion of TB-related costs exceeding 20% of household income or expenditure. Determinants, risk factors, and comorbidities relevant to the national TB epidemic, such as HIV, undernutrition, alcohol use disorders, diabetes, and smoking, should be described. The estimated burden of these risk factors in the general population and among TB patients, as well as in key populations, should be summarized with relevant subnational and subpopulation data. The burden of TB in vulnerable populations, such as children, adolescents, the urban poor, indigenous populations, ethnic minorities, migrants, internally displaced persons, prisoners, and mining communities, should be described. For each group, the estimated population size, TB burden (including drug-resistant TB), and treatment coverage should be detailed, along with recent trends. Data should be disaggregated by age group, gender, and site of TB (pulmonary versus extrapulmonary). The national TB program (NTP) should be described, including its organization at national and subnational levels, with a focus on key interventions in the strategic plan. The organization of services along the TB care cascade should be summarized, covering TB prevention, screening, diagnosis, treatment, support, and care for affected individuals. Relevant technical guidelines for the continuum of care should be referenced. TB infection prevention and control (IPC) measures should be described, focusing on airborne infection control. This includes guidelines, institutional arrangements, and implementation at various levels of the health system and in community and congregate settings. Specific aspects include infection control risk assessments, health facility maintenance, supply mechanisms for IPC resources, and the adequacy of healthcare infrastructure for implementing TB IPC. The national policy on TB preventive treatment (TPT) should be summarized, including TPT regimens, testing for TB infection, target populations, coverage, and uptake. Mechanisms to support adherence to TPT and monitoring and evaluation (M&E) of TPT, including adverse drug events and treatment completion, should be included. The management of TB/HIV co-infection should be described, including coordination mechanisms, data systems, procurement and supply systems, national guidelines for screening and diagnosis, service coverage, treatment outcomes, and the level of decentralization and integration of TB and HIV services. The review of the implementation of the previous TB strategic plan should summarize progress, key achievements, enabling factors, challenges, and recommendations. Gaps in TB service delivery across the care cascade and in coordination within the health sector and other relevant sectors should be identified. The management of TB in children and adolescents should be described, including institutional arrangements for providing health services along the continuum of care. This includes services for contact investigation, availability of child-friendly anti-TB drug formulations, models of care, nutritional and social support, and M&E. Key gaps in the TB program should be identified and quantified where possible. Examples include low coverage of TPT among eligible household contacts, inadequate supplies of TPT medicines, limited health worker capacity, and insufficient data on TB burden in vulnerable populations. Challenges in TB screening, diagnosis, treatment, and care, as well as gaps in addressing comorbidities and nutrition needs, should also be highlighted. The goals of the strategic plan should align with the national vision for ending TB and the End TB Strategy. Goals should be specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and time-bound (SMART). Objectives and strategic interventions should address identified gaps and be logically linked to the goals. Activities and subactivities should be itemized to facilitate costing and implementation, with annual reviews ensuring relevance and responsiveness to the prevailing situation. The M&E component of the NSP should outline indicators to track progress and coordinate M&E activities. Continuous M&E and periodic reviews should be conducted to identify implementation challenges and bottlenecks, enabling timely interventions to improve program performance.
